abstract.text: We focus on the utilisation of reactive trajectory imitation controllers for goal-directed mobile robot navigation. We propose a topological navigation graph (TNG) - an imitationlearning-based framework for navigating through environments with intersecting trajectories. The TNG framework represents the environment as a directed graph composed of deep neural networks. Each vertex of the graph corresponds to a trajectory and is represented by a trajectory identification classifier and a trajectory imitation controller. For trajectory following, we propose the novel use of neural object detection architectures. The edges of TNG correspond to intersections between trajectories and are all represented by a classifier. We provide empirical evaluation of the proposed navigation framework and its components in simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating that TNG allows us to utilise non-goal-directed, imitation-learning methods for goal-directed autonomous navigation.

thesis.text: A topological navigation graph made of learned trajectory controllers and classifiers can turn non-goal-directed imitation-learning skills into goal-directed mobile robot navigation through intersecting trajectories.

On the other side, when humans learn various complex sensorimotor behaviours, including the skill to navigate, adaptivity and imitation play crucial roles [5].
Once children learn several basic behaviours, they soon figure out how to connect them in order to reach different, increasingly complex goals [6].
For more than three decades, artificial neural networks have been utilised to build autonomous mobility systems or their components [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13].
For example, [10] applies behaviour cloning and modern convolutional neural networks (CNNs), achieving vehicle autonomy on real roads,
[14] describes a transfer learning architecture for learning to drive a real vehicle solely in a simulator,
[15] contributes a neural architecture for conditional imitation learning,
[16] introduces a method to learn navigation policies from self-supervision,
[17] proposes a recurrent neural network-based solution

These works, in various aspects, also rely on imitation learning, which highlights a tendency that, by benefiting from the current renaissance of connectionist systems, imitation learning is becoming an increasingly popular robot autonomy research direction [18].
However, many imitation learning algorithms (e.g. [10, 14, 19]) are not goal directed by design.

The main contributions of this study include the TNG framework, the application of neural object detection architectures to obtain more robust trajectory imitation, and the experimental evaluation of the suggested algorithms both in a simulator and the real world by using Neurotechnology’s SentiBotics mobile robot development kit [20].
The problem of learning imitation controllers has a long history [7] and is currently being actively researched [10, 21, 15, 16, 22, 14].
Our first model is derived from [10] which regresses motor commands with the use of a CNN, followed by our second model which is based on an object detection neural network.

We optimise (2) with the Adam optimisation algorithm [28].
As compared to similar work by [10], where the entire parameter set is optimised, our approach helps to reduce the training duration without affecting the performance.

Following the insights of [15] we also use dataset aggregation (DAgger [29]) and augmentation (input/output shifting, random lighting, and regional dropout), allowing us to improve the model’s stability and robustness.

Firstly, controllers trained with this approach are highly sensitive to rotational errors; that is, slight deviations from the trajectory may cause cascading errors [18] and eventually drive the robot out of the trajectory with no possibility of self-recovery.

Thirdly, the trajectory following performance during execution does not necessarily correlate with the value of offline evaluation over the test set using the loss function [30], hence complicating the model evaluation.
In order to solve the aforementioned problems, we utilize the RetinaNet object detection architecture [31].
Conceptually, our approach is similar to that of [22].
The model used for training is pre-trained on the COCO dataset [32] over the object detection task.

During controller execution, the output of the object detector (i.e. coordinates of the bounding box showing the direction of movement) is coupled with a PID controller [33] to centre a detected bounding box, resulting in trajectory imitation.
The work from [11], which includes a mapper and a planner, advances previous approaches.
A noteworthy feature of [11] is that their method is able to generalize to new environments.
Another approach [13], proposes a semi-parametric topological memory (SPTM) architecture for navigation, where the environment is mapped on a non-parametric graph, in which every position is a node.
[34] attempts to tackle the challenge of learning goal-directed policies from data representing a single traversal in an environment spanning over 2 kilometres.
Whilst end-to-end learning can simultaneously tune the entire architecture’s parameter set, this advantage often comes at the cost of requiring large datasets and longer training durations [35].

Reinforcement learning-based methods such as [11] are dependent on high amounts of resources for training its joint architecture since it needs to tune the parameters by interacting with a well-mapped, photo-realistic environment.
While [34] is also a reinforcement-learning-based method, to reduce the resource-heavy factor it leverages the method with one-shot reinforcement learning [36].
[13] relies on self-supervised learning but no real-world demonstrations have been shown in the work.

After the shortest path in the TNG between current and target vertices is computed (e.g. by Dijkstra’s algorithm [37]), we can start executing the controllers and classifiers, contained in its vertices and edges, switching them at every intersection connecting towards the goal, recognised by corresponding intersection classifiers until the goal trajectory is reached.

The parameters of the classification network, θ, are optimised by minimising cross entropy loss [23], and the parameters of the encoder network, ˆ ξ, are pre-trained on the ImageNet [26] classification task and kept fixed during training of trajectory imitation controller.
We select MobileNetV2 [25] because it allows us to achieve an acceptable execution speed using low cost embedded neural network inference hardware⁴.

In order to minimise manual data labelling in our implementation, we perform the learning of intersections with the use of a proprietary object recognition engine derived from [38], using FAST corners [39] and BRIEF features [40] as descriptors.
Our implementation of trajectory imitation controllers and TNG is performed with the use of Neurotechnology’s SentiBotics Navigation SDK 3.0 [20].
To compare the performance of trajectory imitation controllers we use percentage autonomy [10] as a controller quality measure:

We also noticed the object detection based controllers with better loss over the test sets show better real-world performances, which is not the case for the regression controller [30], this can be further investigated in future work.

In contrast to metric models (e.g. [2, 11, 3]), where localisation is performed by geometrically estimating a robot’s pose on a map, or to other topological (e.g. [13, 41, 34]) or hybrid (e.g. [42, 43]) approaches, the trajectory classifiers and trajectory intersection classifiers of TNG provide only minimal localisation information, required to keep or switch reactive behaviour in a way that eventually leads to reaching the given goal.

sections.summary: Motivates the need for goal-directed robot navigation and argues that imitation-learning controllers are useful but not goal directed by design. It introduces TNG and lists the three contributions.
sections.title: Introduction and Contributions

sections.summary: Defines trajectory imitation controllers, then compares a CNN regression controller with an object-detection-based controller. The regression controller minimises ridge loss after behaviour cloning and DAgger, while the object-detection controller detects a bounding box for movement direction and uses a PID controller.
sections.title: Learning Trajectory Imitation Controllers

sections.summary: Reviews related topological, end-to-end, and reinforcement-learning navigation work, then formalises TNG as a directed graph whose vertices and edges are classifiers and controllers. It also describes implementation choices for classifiers, goal-reaching, and the two controller variants.
sections.title: Topological Navigation Graph Framework and Implementation

sections.summary: Describes the four evaluation environments and data collection, then compares the regression and object-detection controllers using percentage autonomy before and after a four-week interval. The object-detection controller degrades less under environmental change.
sections.title: Evaluation Setup and Reactive Controller Experiments

sections.summary: Evaluates full TNG navigation on five office trajectories with randomly selected start and goal positions, reporting percentage autonomy and travelled distance. It argues TNG enables goal-directed navigation while noting modularity, interpretability, and limitations such as geometric sub-optimality and the intersecting-trajectory assumption.
sections.title: TNG Goal-Directed Navigation Experiments

sections.summary: Concludes that object-detection architectures can be used for visuomotor trajectory imitation and that TNG composes reactive controllers into a goal-directed navigation system. Future work includes more reliable imitation learning, automatic graph construction, and a hierarchical component.
sections.title: Conclusion and Future Work

abstract.text: We focus on the utilisation of reactive trajectory imitation controllers for goal-directed mobile robot navigation. We propose a topological navigation graph (TNG) - an imitationlearning-based framework for navigating through environments with intersecting trajectories. The TNG framework represents the environment as a directed graph composed of deep neural networks. Each vertex of the graph corresponds to a trajectory and is represented by a trajectory identification classifier and a trajectory imitation controller. For trajectory following, we propose the novel use of neural object detection architectures. The edges of TNG correspond to intersections between trajectories and are all represented by a classifier. We provide empirical evaluation of the proposed navigation framework and its components in simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating that TNG allows us to utilise non-goal-directed, imitation-learning methods for goal-directed autonomous navigation.

On the other side, when humans learn various complex sensorimotor behaviours, including the skill to navigate, adaptivity and imitation play crucial roles [5].
Once children learn several basic behaviours, they soon figure out how to connect them in order to reach different, increasingly complex goals [6].
For more than three decades, artificial neural networks have been utilised to build autonomous mobility systems or their components [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13].
For example, [10] applies behaviour cloning and modern convolutional neural networks (CNNs), achieving vehicle autonomy on real roads,
[14] describes a transfer learning architecture for learning to drive a real vehicle solely in a simulator,
[15] contributes a neural architecture for conditional imitation learning,
[16] introduces a method to learn navigation policies from self-supervision,
[17] proposes a recurrent neural network-based solution

These works, in various aspects, also rely on imitation learning, which highlights a tendency that, by benefiting from the current renaissance of connectionist systems, imitation learning is becoming an increasingly popular robot autonomy research direction [18].
However, many imitation learning algorithms (e.g. [10, 14, 19]) are not goal directed by design.

The main contributions of this study include the TNG framework, the application of neural object detection architectures to obtain more robust trajectory imitation, and the experimental evaluation of the suggested algorithms both in a simulator and the real world by using Neurotechnology’s SentiBotics mobile robot development kit [20].
The problem of learning imitation controllers has a long history [7] and is currently being actively researched [10, 21, 15, 16, 22, 14].
Our first model is derived from [10] which regresses motor commands with the use of a CNN, followed by our second model which is based on an object detection neural network.

sections.summary: Motivates the need for goal-directed robot navigation and argues that imitation-learning controllers are useful but not goal directed by design. It introduces TNG and lists the three contributions.
sections.title: Introduction and Contributions

sections.summary: Defines trajectory imitation controllers, then compares a CNN regression controller with an object-detection-based controller. The regression controller minimises ridge loss after behaviour cloning and DAgger, while the object-detection controller detects a bounding box for movement direction and uses a PID controller.
sections.title: Learning Trajectory Imitation Controllers

sections.summary: Reviews related topological, end-to-end, and reinforcement-learning navigation work, then formalises TNG as a directed graph whose vertices and edges are classifiers and controllers. It also describes implementation choices for classifiers, goal-reaching, and the two controller variants.
sections.title: Topological Navigation Graph Framework and Implementation

sections.summary: Describes the four evaluation environments and data collection, then compares the regression and object-detection controllers using percentage autonomy before and after a four-week interval. The object-detection controller degrades less under environmental change.
sections.title: Evaluation Setup and Reactive Controller Experiments

sections.summary: Evaluates full TNG navigation on five office trajectories with randomly selected start and goal positions, reporting percentage autonomy and travelled distance. It argues TNG enables goal-directed navigation while noting modularity, interpretability, and limitations such as geometric sub-optimality and the intersecting-trajectory assumption.
sections.title: TNG Goal-Directed Navigation Experiments

sections.summary: Concludes that object-detection architectures can be used for visuomotor trajectory imitation and that TNG composes reactive controllers into a goal-directed navigation system. Future work includes more reliable imitation learning, automatic graph construction, and a hierarchical component.
sections.title: Conclusion and Future Work
